items.heading: Young Belgravians on the world stage
items.summary: Round-up of Belgrave athletes at the 2003 European U23 and U20 Championships, World Student Games and World Youth Championships, led by Chris Lambert's European U23 200m and Universiade 100m titles, with results lines; the report says the GB U23 sprint relay won in 39.54 while the results line gives GBR 39.31 and BEL 39.54.
items.text:
European U23 Championships, Bydgoszcz, Poland, 17-20 July 2003.
The 2003 season marked a big step forward for Chris Lambert. Troubled by hamstring injuries in recent seasons, Chris put his worries behind him and produced the goods for himself and coach John Powell, by racing to the gold medal in the European U23 Championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland. Facing the home-crowd favourite Marcin Jedrusinski, who was fifth in last year's European Championship in Munich, Chris ran a perfectly controlled bend to enter the straight on his rival's shoulder. A relaxed, powerful finish then brought him through to victory in the last few metres. The winning time of 20.34 was a personal record and also a full tenth and more inside the previous championship best.

Chris also shared in the golden glory achieved by the GB 4 x 100 metres squad. The qualifying round saw a British team that was three-quarters Belgrave scrape into the final after a near disaster when lead-off runner Grant ran into a slowly starting Lambert. But Belgrave team mates Darren Chin and Tim Abeyie (who also ran in the individual 200m) pulled the quartet into the last qualifying position. Tim was replaced in the final by Edgar, to leave the team a mere 50% Belgrave, and this time all went well as they headed the French side by 7/100ths to win in 39.54.

Tim Benjamin set his best ever time of 45.71 to win his 400 metres heat but lining up for the final was feeling less than 100% as he prepared to do battle with the French European Junior Champion Leslie Djhone. In fact the Frenchman ran a scintillating race and Tim had his work cut out to pursue, and finally overtake, the Pole Wieruszewski and claim the silver medal. The Belgrave man later admitted that Djhone would surely still have been the winner, even if he had felt better on the day, but he may have run a shade faster.

Goldie Sayers placed 11th in the Javelin, not so far behind her season's best, but Scot Thompson was out of sorts as he was only able to manage 48.89 in the discus, some 7 metres down on his best for the year. Dominic Girdler had an injury problem and was unable to compete in the sprint hurdles.

European U20 Championships, Tampere, Finland, 24-27 July 2003
Amy Spencer had been suffering from knee problems leading into the games but nevertheless was able to equal her outdoor 200m best of 23.45 as she won her first round race - the fastest of all the qualifiers. In the final she was battling for a medal as she entered the straight but faded a little and had to be content with fourth. No doubt a silver medal in the relay went some way towards relieving her disappointment.

Unfortunately, the previous winner of the women's 200 metre title, our own Vernicha James, was unable to take her place in the line-up for the 2003 championship, having been unable to rid herself of the hamstring injury that has been dogging her since the indoor season.

In the men's 200 metres James Ellington placed 2nd in his heat behind the 100m champion Helmke of Germany, his time of 21.36 being his second fastest ever for the distance. In a highly competitive final James went faster still and placed 6th, just 2/100ths outside his lifetime best, with 4th to 6th places all within 1/100th of a second.

The mighty Laurence Oboh has had his winter conditioning plagued by injury but it's now looking as if he has put those problems behind him. His powerful back-straight run in the sprint relay put the British team right into contention and with two 100 metre finalists to follow the team powered to a win over Germany to claim the gold medals.

World Student Games Champs., Daegu, Korea, 25-30 August
Again Chris Lambert came up with the goods as he put together a winning string from heats to final to win the World Universiade 100 metres.

Matt Douglas ran to the silver medal in the 400 metre hurdles with a time that probably would have pleased him had he not set an astounding mark two days earlier. In winning his semi-final in 48.54 Matt became the fourth fastest Briton of all time behind Akabusi, Hemery and Rawlinson. The time is also inside the qualifying mark for the 2004 Olympic Games. A bronze was added to his silver medal as he helped the British 4x400 metre team to third place.

World Youth Champs, Sherbrooke, Canada, 10 July 2003
Olympians of the future gathered in Canada for the third edition of what has become known as "the Under-18 Olympics". Our 16 year-old giant Chris Gearing rose to the occasion to heave the shot a mighty 18.70 for a personal best and to qualify for the full six rounds of the final.

items.summary: Editorial on the busy 2003 season and the club's new track and field league plans: leaving the Thameside and Women's Southern Leagues, joining the UK Women's League and the new London Inter-Club Challenge.
items.text:
It feels that this issue is hot on the heels of the last one, but there is certainly no shortage of material to fill it - it has been such a busy summer. Naturally track & field has the lion's share of the coverage, but latterly there has been great success on the roads as well to report, particularly the string of important wins in the relays. Although we have included general results right up to the end of November, we have been unable to squeeze in the cross country relays and Surrey CC League events - these will follow in the next issue, hopefully due out in May 2004, when the winter and spring season is complete. In that issue we also plan to include the 2003 club ranking lists and the start of a series which will record some of the history of our club.

This year saw the re-emergence of the junior men in the National Junior League and they also contributed to a record seventh win for the seniors in the British Athletics League (BAL). The senior women, as well as again triumphing with the men in winning the BAL Golden Jubilee Cup, also capped their season with qualification for the UK Womens League (UKWL) and this, together with major developments in our track & field programme, means that next summer's fixtures will have a new look.

In the light of these new developments we have decided not to continue with the Thameside League for our Under 13 and Under 15 athletes, although rest assured they will be catered for in our more structured programme. We would like to take this opportunity, therefore, to thank all those who have played their part in organising the Thameside over the last 21 seasons - in particular Derek Crookes who has been in the midst of its administration since the league's inception in 1983.

The new developments to which we have referred have been triggered by the prospect of our women competing in the UK Women's League. This competition is for seniors only. We could have continued to compete in the Women's Southern League as well, which additionally includes U15 and limited U17 competition, but with our top senior athletes unlikely to devote as much time to the WSL as they would like, we would be faced with difficulties in sustaining two teams where much travel is involved.

Additional complications were provided by the National Junior Athletics League planning to go mixed in 2005 and the fact that the National Young Athletes League had already become a competition for both boys and girls in 2003.

We believe that our new plan is just the thing to offer meaningful competition to all our T&F athletes whatever their age.

We will be pulling out of the Women's Southern League but have become founder members of a new competition - the London Inter-Club Challenge (LICC). At the time of writing this is planned for women only - but discussions are ongoing regarding an equivalent men's event. This competition will start by offering four matches per season, all of which will take place inside the M25. Up to ten athletes per club will be allowed to compete in each event with the best two scoring in the match. There will be no relegation or promotion but a challenge trophy will be awarded to the overall winning team at the conclusion of the fourth match. There will be no barring clauses. Athletes who compete in the three UKWL matches will be able to benefit from the extra competition if they wish while, with up to ten per event, athletes of a more modest standard will also get the competition they require. There will be limited competition in these matches for U17 and U15 athletes.

Our successful National Junior League Men will be joined in the Brent Division by our first ever Under 20 Women's team. Although the men's and women's points will not be amalgamated to provide the division winner in 2004 - they will be in 2005. And to form the 2005 Southern Premier Division the best four combined men's and women's teams in that division in 2004 will remain in it but that leaves four places open for the best combined men's and women's teams from all the other divisions - including ours. Under 20s will also be permitted to compete in senior competition in the LICC, or indeed the UKWL or BAL, should they be selected.

We have reapplied to join the National Young Athletes League - five matches where boys and girls will be able to enjoy the full range of competition in their own age-groups - U17, U15 and U13. Those in the U17 age groups will also be permitted to take part in the National Junior League.

But that's for the future - read on to to see how your Club has fared during the long hot summer of 2003.

And please write in with your comments, or submit articles for publication. We don't have a 'Letters' page because no-one writes to us!

items.heading: From “The Belgravian”
items.summary: Column recalling what The Belgravian reported 75, 50 and 25 years earlier: the club badge debate, cross-country, relay and race walking successes, and Frank Elson's death.
items.text:
75 Years ago

A letter to the Editor in the first issue of the year referred to the possible origin of the Club badge. The writer, who signed himself "Cocoanut", gave proof that the badge was derived from the arms of the City of Westminster and that the cross keys possibly denoted that St Peter was the patron saint of Belgrave! One suspects that the writer ought to have signed himself "Chestnut" as the matter is still a topic of conversation.

Our runners won the Surrey Cross Country Championships for the third time in four years, the team being led home by Arthur Penny. A month later and we triumphed in the South of the Thames at Gatton Park, Reigate, plus taking the trophy for the first club with twelve men home. A very fitting win as Harry Hare the Club President held the same office for the South of the Thames.

Just to add to the letter from "Cocoanut" another correspondent "Full Circle" made the observation that the Club motto meant "Ever Ready" because our ancestors foresaw that the Club would eventually produce leading lights in the athletic world. You can say that again!

The National Cross Country Championship at Beaconsfield was run in a blizzard which caused many to drop out including half our team but we bounced back in the Brighton relay where with four men setting Club records we managed seventh place gaining medals for the most improved team.

The only National Road Walk Championship in those days was over 20 miles and the critics felt we had little chance so it was all the sweeter to take first place with Tommy Green leading the way and one the early editors of the magazine, Ben Knifton, as fourth scoring man.

Early track fixtures included a match against London AC at Battersea in which Lord Burghley appeared for the host Club and the subsequent Inter Club Relay Meeting gave us an easy win. A Club 880 yards handicap received 61 entries - a Club and possibly National record for turn out and the final was won in just over 2 minutes.

50 Years Ago

The July issue started with the tragic news that the Editor and Club President, Frank Elson, had died. The consequential debate as to the format and finances for the magazine led to the proposal to charge for the Belgravian. Almost a year had passed since the previous issue and so space was at a premium. We finished third in the Surrey County Road Relay and it is interesting to note that the team included Bill Lucas, Arthur Bruce, Charlie Walker and Len Bishop all still seen at the Hall from time to time! Add to these Bob Taylor who saw us home in second place the Mitcham to Brighton Relay and you have the feeling that not much changes in 50 years. In the National Relay from Westminster to Brighton we finished second to SLH just over 2 minutes behind and there was a plea, from Bill Lucas, that we needed younger blood to replace the older members of the team - 5 of the team were over 35.

The National Cross Country Championships saw us field teams in all the races then held. We were 9th in the Senior, 16th in the Junior with G Biscoe in the team, and 8th in the Youths with George Flanagan in the scoring four.

On the track the Leyton Floodlit Meeting on a cold blustery evening saw Dennis Merrett, Ted Gaworski, John Bromley and Bob Taylor among a good Club turn out. County Championship results recorded 7 wins, 7 seconds and 7 thirds - all very regular and names included Basil Walden in addition to some noted above. Bob Taylor equalled the Middlesex record held by the great Arthur Wint in the 880 yards, and Ivan Mayers beat Ron Holtum in the sprints while Jack Brown won the Kent one mile.

The walkers had their triumphs, none more so than Norman Guilmant over the longer distances who after his second place in the Brighton won international colours in Italy where he, unfortunately, collapsed but no lasting harm was done. Team building was the message and steady progress was made in all the Open walks which boded well for the future. The longer distance men did their stuff and we won the National 20 in which George Beecham won the first of many winning team medals.

25 Years Ago

The Editor bemoaned the lack of pack training and saw as one problem the fact that our membership was drawn from a very wide area - more true than ever today. One of the incentives mentioned in "Grapevine" was that Haig the distillers who sponsored our Road Relay had upped the team prize from a gallon of the "hard stuff" to a bottle for each member of the team!

Very good turn outs were to be found in the Boys, Youths and Colts events with John Gladwin and Mark Sinclair featuring in teams with the latter finishing 30th in the Surrey Cross Country Youths Championships. Our Seniors were not having too good a time and were finding life difficult in the Surrey League and most of the photographs show snowbound fields which may have accounted for some of the problems.

"With the Ladies" included a health warning to the effect that we lacked coaches and ought to pay particular attention to this. The lady walkers had success in various races including third place in the National. With Wendy Dunsford as team Field Events Captain, we were well set. Club President, Ray Middleton, was turning out along with Richard Dorman, Paul Blagg and Carl Lawton to keep the walking flag flying although it was the first occasion on which we failed to have a team in the Brighton. Doug Fotheringham was, then as now, still striding round and although we won the several titles we missed our own Open walk by just one point.

The back cover of the magazine featured a trio of runners who completed the Harlow Unigate Marathon the centre one being John Davies, another still seen around the Hall on occasion.

Just as we go to print we regret to inform you of the death of the Club's oldest member.

Arthur Penny, gold medallist at 6 miles in the 1934 Empire Games died on Saturday 29th November in Kingston Hospital. He was just a few days short of his 96th birthday and was in his 76th year as a Belgravian.

A full tribute to Arthur will appear in the next issue.

items.heading: Hon. Secretary's Report to A.G.M. 2003
items.summary: The General Secretary's report to the 2003 AGM reviewing track and field, race walking, road, cross country and individual international achievements, the club's new CASC status and trading company, and prospects for the coming season.
items.text:
Success breeds success and, following on from what Alan Mead described in his report to the AGM in 2002 as the "most successful year in our 115 year history", then the last twelve months have certainly not been a disappointment.

Track & Field
In our track and field teams, the men's British League team dominated yet again, winning not only all four matches, but also the British League title for the 7th consecutive year. They have now won this title more than any other club, though we still must win next year if we are to equal the marvellous eight consecutive victories of Wolverhampton & Bilston. Our women, although finishing in the bottom half of the table in Southern Division 1, were offered the opportunity to compete in the UK Women's League qualifier match earlier this month. This was as a result of their performances in the Jubilee Cup. Despite only seven days' notice, and missing many of their leading internationals, they convincingly won the match, thanks to the great effort and commitment shown by all those taking part, and have now gained that all important promotion to the UK Women's League.

In Lisbon, the men once again represented the UK in the European Champion Clubs Cup and finished 6th of eight teams, and in conjunction with the ladies team, we retained the Jubilee Cup, now in its second year.

Success, however, does come at a price. With many of our men either taking part in international competitions or competing at national level, our men's Southern League team, after relegation to Division 2 last year, finished in the bottom part of the table.

Our Junior men now seem to be coming into some good form under the leadership of Gerald Sprigings. They won their final junior league match and with many of the juniors already experiencing senior and international competitions so we have a bright future ahead of us. Last winter the Youths and Boys team won the Surrey Cross Country League and they are looking to repeat that success in the coming winter.

Race Walking
Our race walking section has seen no material changes over the previous year. Unlike in our other senior sections and also our masters where we have younger competitors coming through, our race walking section struggles to attract new blood, a problem faced by the sport as a whole in this country. However, our walkers continue to enjoy and are very enthusiastic about their sport and surely it must be time to put a little more emphasis into this section, which boasts Belgrave's only Olympic gold medallist.

Road Running
In road running, the men have again continued their reign of success by retaining both their National 12 Stage and National 6 Stage titles, in addition, on the way to those achievements, also retaining the Southern 12 stage title and winning the Southern 6 stage title for the first time ever. The men were also second in both the AAAs 10 km and Half Marathon Championships, as well as placing 9th in the European Champion Clubs Cup Half Marathon in Almada, Portugal - the first time Belgrave had been asked to represent the UK in a road competition.

The ladies team is also continuing to improve. Although the ladies were not medallists at Southern or National level last year, it is now only a matter of time before they are enjoying success similar to the men's team and they are looking forward to the new year ahead with great enthusiasm and team spirit.

Cross Country
In the cross country section, we struggled in the men's Surrey League, finishing 3rd, although this does follow the pattern of previous years - 1st, 3rd, 1st, 3rd, so perhaps this year we can look forward to regaining that title! In the major Southern and National Championships, we finished well below our potential, and this is the one area where we need to encourage everyone to turn out and represent the Club, so that we can aim to be crowned National Champions over the country as well as on the road. Although no significant victories for the ladies cross country team, they are now firmly established in Surrey League Division 1 and have high hopes for the forthcoming season.

We should take this opportunity to thank all the team managers for their invaluable contribution and for all the time and effort they put into running these teams. Of course, we should also thank our sponsors, adidas, for their continued support of the Club and our supporters and helpers who follow the teams across Europe.

Individual Performances
Now turning to individual performances, in the major worldwide championships, seven Belgravians qualified for the World Athletic Championships; Sean Baldock, Tim Benjamin, Dwain Chambers, (who achieved a silver medal in the 4 x 100 m), Julie Hollman, Rachel King, Shelley Newman and Amy Spencer. In the World Indoor Championships, we were represented by Tim Benjamin, (a bronze medallist in the 4 x 400 m), Sarah Claxton, Rachel King, Chris Moss and Amy Spencer. Vernicha James was also selected but had to withdraw due to injury.

In the World Student Games, we were represented by Chris Lambert (won gold in the 100 m), Matt Douglas (won silver in the 400m hurdles and bronze in the 4x400 m relay), Goldie Sayers and Michelle Carey. In the European U23 Championships, we were represented by Tim Abeyie (gold 4x100 m), Tim Benjamin (silver 400 m), Darren Chin (gold 4 x 100 m), Dominic Girdler, Chris Lambert (gold 200 m and 4 x 100 m), Samson Oni, Goldie Sayers and Scot Thompson. In the European U20 Championships, we were represented by James Ellington and Amy Spencer. In the European Youth Olympic Festival, we were represented by Wade Bennett-Jackson, who took gold in both the 100 m and 200 m, Amala Onuora and Chris Gearing.

In the World Cross Country Championships, we were represented in the long course by Spencer Barden and Mark Miles. In the European Cross Country Championships, we were represented by Spencer Barden and Allen Graffin in the long course, as well as Jonathan Blackledge in the junior race.

Of course, many more of our members, across the age groups and events, have produced fine performances, winning county, area and national championships. All these details can be found on our website and in the Belgravian magazine. Thanks should be given to Alan Mead and all those who contribute to these important publications.

General Matters
I now turn to some more general matters relating to the Club. Following an EGM in February this year, Belgrave Harriers have now gained Community Amateur Sports Club status. What this basically means is that we now have charitable status and for every £1 donated to the Club from taxed income, we are able to claim a further 28p from the government.

In April this year, we set up and incorporated Belgrave Sports Promotions Limited - known simply as BsportsP. This is a trading company, the profits from which are utilised wholly for the benefit of Belgrave Harriers. The Company is run on a voluntary basis by members of the Committee and all the shares in the Company are held by Belgrave's Trustee's on behalf of Belgrave Harriers.

So what about the immediate future? We have already made a good start a few weeks ago, with the men's team winning the Surrey Road Relays for the first time since 1997 and our ladies winning bronze, with Angela Walker setting a new course record on the way. This weekend, we will be at Aldershot where the men will be defending their Southern 6 stage title and the women will be aiming to win their first medals in the 4 stage competition. If we can keep the momentum going we'll be heading to Sutton Park as favourites to win the Men's National 6 stage for the 3rd consecutive year, with a highest ever placing on the cards for the ladies.

With all this success, we should not forget that there are many other people who give their time voluntarily to the Club and to the sport as a whole, often taking on small roles which are invaluable to the running of the Club and I would like to take this opportunity to thank those individuals, particularly to the team of cleaners, who came to the rescue when the Hall was without a regular cleaner last year. The success of the Club as a whole relies on all the individuals who devote their spare time. We are always seeking more volunteers and if you think you can assist in any way, however small, then please do come forward. It is due to the time and effort given by all the volunteers and the athletes who are competing for us, that we are now enjoying such a sustained period of success, of which we can all be very proud. Long may it continue.

Roger Alsop, General Secretary, September 2003

items.heading: Helsinki 1983 versus Paris 2003
items.summary: Rex Bale recalls attending the first IAAF World Championships in Helsinki in 1983 and compares its performances with the 2003 Championships in Paris.
items.text:
Rex Bale recalls his visit to the first IAAF World Championships in Helsinki twenty years ago and compares some of the performances with those in Paris.

The first World Championships were dominated by the USA for the Men and the Eastern Bloc countries but with enough British successes to keep the UK contingent happy. Daley Thompson, Steve Cram, Kathy Cook and Fatima Whitbread were prominent. In the heptathlon Judy Livermore (Simpson) had her moments too, notably jumping 6 cms higher than her three closest rivals who included Jackie Joyner who went on to do great things. Judy's 1.92 metres would have placed her fifth in the individual event. However on Day 2, I saw her out shopping for souvenirs and signing autographs in her 'lunch break' and wondered if this was the best preparation for her final afternoon's efforts to grab a medal - perhaps not, as she had three no-throws in the javelin and decided to skip the final event, the 800 metres.

I cannot recall a single controversy in Helsinki. Certainly the only athletes seen lying on the track were not protesting but writhing in agony. We were prevented from seeing a head-to-head in the womens 100m between Evelyn Ashford (USA) and Marlies Gohr (GDR) since poor Evelyn suffered a hamstring tear 30 metres down the straight in the final. Alberto Jauantorena of Cuba, winner of the 400/800 Olympic double in 1976 and now a member of the IAAF Council, was another victim. He tore two ankle ligaments when he stepped onto the kerbing after just managing to qualify for the semi finals as a fastest loser.

Comparing the standards with the Paris there were some remarkable similarities and some drastic differences. Women's hurdling appears to have stood still since in both Championships the first five ran under 12.8 seconds for the 100m and the first six under 55 seconds for the 400m. Furthermore the winner in Paris was the slowest ever (12.53). The men's long jump finals were also similar with seven men over eight metres in both Championhips, although Carl Lewis' spectacular opening leap of 8.55 metres in Helsinki stood apart from the rest. It was a different story in the women's event where the first four jumped longer than Eunice Barber in Paris. These four included 18 years old Heike Daute (Dreschler) who won the gold, and Carol Lewis, sister of Carl, now embarking on a career as a B movie actor.

Both the Helsinki 1500m and 5000m were slow tactical races to such an extent that the last man in Paris would have beaten gold medallist Steve Cram by three seconds, and in the 5000m thirteen runners bettered Eamon Coughlan's winning time. The differences in the winning times were 10 seconds in the case of Crammy's race and a massive 35 seconds in the case of Ireland's Coughlan who must be the only Championship winner to give a victory salute 150 metres from the finish while lying in second place! In the 1500m Spain's Jose Abascal led the procession with 65, 63 and 60 seconds laps and Said Aouita sped for home with 39 seconds for the last 300m but was overhauled by Cram and by Steve Scott of the USA who always seemed to miss out at the big Championships.

Hestri Cloete of South Africa was an emphatic high jump winner with 2.06 in Paris, but the event appeared (on TV at least) to lack the excitement in Helsinki where an enthralled crowd stayed well past 9pm to see Russian Tamara Bykova (2.01) finally victorious over West Germany's Ulrike Meyfarth (1.99) with black and white USA represented by Colleen Sommer and Louise Ritter (1.95). I recall that a group of Americans remained seated during the Russian national anthem and were jeered by we Brits sitting behind them - the Cold War was still raging then after all.

The steeplechase has come on a little with the Kenyans now putting the event on a different level. In Helsinki Patrick Ilg of Germany contributed to that country's best ever World Championships by winning in 8:15 with Britain's Colin Reitz third. But in spite of the apparently suicidal uneven pace in Paris the first seven were still faster and the winning time of the self-exiled Kenyan from Qatar was over 10 seconds better.

The marathon brought out a CBP from Gharib of Morocco (2:08.31) this time around but in depth Helsinki was a good match with nine under 2:11.15, including our own Hugh Jones, and fourteen breaking that time in Paris.

The times in three of the four relays were closely matched. In the Men's 4x100 the USA may have sneaked a win at the expense of the GB quartet in Paris but they did not quite better the world record time of 37.86 set by the USA team in Helsinki. No wonder since this team included the three 100m medallists - Carl Lewis, Calvin Smith and Emmit King - and the 110mH bronze medallist, Willie Gault. The Women's 4x400m was the exception since the USA team's time in Paris was the slowest in the history of the Championhips and would not have gained them a medal in Helsinki where the Eastern Bloc countries of East Germany, Czechoslovakia and Russia filled the top three slots.

Apart from Aouita and Joyner other stars in the ascendency in Helsinki were Sergei Bubka making his breakthrough in the pole vault at 19 years old. Merlene Ottey (4th in the 100m), the late Florence Griffiths-Joyner ('Flo-Jo' - 4th in the 200m), and Silke Gladisch (Muller) - sprint relay gold medallist.

There were also some former stars who were beginning to fade including those great sprinters Pietro Mennea and Allan Wells (third and fourth in the 200m), and John Walker (NZ) and Mike Boit (Kenya) - ninth and twelth in the 1500m.

The Worlds return to Helsinki in 2005 and anyone thinking of going should beware of drastic weather changes. In August 1983 a heatwave in the first half of Championhips week was followed by sharply dropping tempertures in the second half and by the end of the week the night temperature dropped below freezing. Rain too lashed down to such an extent that the pole vault qualifying competition was abandoned. I for one was wearing all the clothes I took on the last two days in the magnificent but almost roofless stadium. Fortunately a roof is promised for 2005 !

items.heading: Paul King stars in Roubaix 28 hour Walk
items.summary: Carl Lawton reports Paul King becoming the first Belgravian to complete the Roubaix 28 hour walk, placing 26th with 191.525 km.
items.text:
Carl Lawton writes: Paul King competed in the Roubaix 28 hour walk on Saturday and Sunday 20/21 September and became the first Belgravian to complete the course in its 50 years. Starting at 1pm on the Saturday with an entourage of the local band riding bicycles, the 87 competitors did a 20km circuit of the outskirts of the town in extremely hot conditions before going onto the 4 km circuit which certainly was not traffic free.

This was a full international race with competitors from all over Europe and Paul had been selected to represent England after his performance at Newmarket over 100 miles a few weeks earlier.

As the race progressed into the night Paul kept plugging away and gained a few places as some of the faster starters tired and fell back. By midnight it had cooled and additional clothes were added and warmer drinks provided. The morning turned quite chilly but still the miles (kms) were added and numbers decreased due to retirements - but Paul was still going. Peter Ryan (Sheffield) the winner at Newmarket had retired and Ian Statter, 3rd at Newmarket, was not going well and was behind Paul. Breakfast was taken by the English support team, some of whom had managed a couple of hours sleep, as the walkers pressed on. The noon sun was again hot and there were still 5 hours to go. Paul was in about 30th position and numbers had fallen to about 60. At about 23 hours Paul reached the 100 mile point.

With one and half hours to go the walkers were transferred to a 900m circuit. Up and down the High Street before finishing at 5pm with a large crowd in attendance.

Paul finally crossed the line in 28 hours 3 mins 47 secs covering 191.525kms, (119miles.) for an excellent 26th position. The winner was Grzegorz-Adam Urbanowski from Poland who covered 242kms and our first English competitor home was Sandra Brown (Surrey WC) in 6th place 222kms.

items.heading: The Backroom Boy
items.summary: Alan Mead's profile of new club President Don Anderson, tracing his life from Croydon schoolboy and Army steeplechaser to Surrey AC, the 1982 amalgamation with Belgrave and years as the club's indispensable helper and timing officer.
items.text:
Don Anderson, President of Belgrave Harriers 2003-3004 by Alan Mead

The Backroom Boy

It's 10 o'clock and the night is foul. A rising wind rattles the letterbox and hurls rain against the windows with a staccato patter. "What a night!" But thoughts of pity for anyone out in such conditions are interrupted by the chiming of the doorbell. "For goodness sake! Who can that be!" The struggle to open the door, apparently gripped on the other side by some fiend of the night, is finally won and standing, dripping, in the porch, waterproofs and crash helmet glistening in the streetlights, is ... Don Anderson.

He's come to collect the flags so that he can get an early start tomorrow in marking the course for the our home Surrey Cross Country League race. And one instantly knows full well that he will mark the course before noon and then remark it when vandals move the flags in an attempt to direct the youngsters race across the golf course fairway; he will turn out to run in the men's race - and then, when everyone else is heading for home, he will go round again to collect the flags up.

It's a similar story of dedication in the heat of the summer. Soon after midday, having taken a half day off work, he'll be up at Battersea rigging the computers ... and cabling ... and camera ... and lighting ... to set everything up for the evening's adidas SPEED Grand Prix. After testing and re-testing, everything at last seems to be working. At 7pm the first wave of sprinters tears down the 100 metre straight. Yes, the clock's running, the wind gauge is registering and in a few tenths beyond 10 seconds the photo electric beam is broken and the electric clock flashes up the winner's time to the 1/100th. The meeting moves on. The middle-distance men come on to do their stuff, dusk falls, the lights over the finish line come on and the sprinters come back for the 200s. Eventually the track is deserted - except for two or three stalwarts, one of them of course being Don. The cable runs have been coiled, scaffolding shifted and barrow-loads of equipment stored away in the club-room. Eight or more hours after arriving at the track he at last gets to leave the park.

Don is the backroom boy to beat all backroom boys. If there's a job to be done then he'll do it. What would we do without such people?

Born in Croydon in 1955, Don moved to New Malden as a youngster and went to Beverley School. Frankly, he wasn't keen on school at all and was far more at home making some spare cash by working at the local greengrocer's. Before long he was rising early to start work as a barrow boy in London's fruit and vegetable market, hauling half a ton of spuds at a time. This hard graft gave him a considerable strength advantage over other boys in his year at school - but it also gave him a few headaches as he struggled into class, late and yawning, with a day's study ahead of him. As he now regretfully admits, his school work suffered, but when it came to activity on the sports field his fitness told and he found himself in Beverley's rugby, cross country and track & field teams. In 1969 he won the Kingston and Surrey Schools 3,000 metres championship.

The sports master at Beverley was one David Philp who encouraged Don to join the local athletic club - Surrey AC - who where in Division One of the newly formed British Athletics League. In the next few years he found himself training for 800s and 1500s with coach Charles Elliott at Crystal Palace. But when it came to competition, Surrey AC were short of 5000 metre and steeplechase men and, as ever, Don slotted in where he was most needed.

The distance runners of Surrey AC, with no cross country base of their own, tended to drift up to Lauriston Cottage - Arthur Whitehead's place on the edge of Wimbledon Common - and at one time Don actually lived at the cottage with a group of other runners.

Upon leaving school Don had stayed at the greengrocers but now, influenced by Arthur, was encouraged to join the Army and in 1975 signed up with the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers where he trained as an electronics engineer. It didn't take the Army long to find out that Don was a runner and could handle some tough going so he was dispatched to Lympstone for a commando course. Don likes things tough - but not necessarily that tough! But it did his running the world of good.

In 1976 he was posted to Arborfield in Berkshire, home to the modern pentathlon squad who won gold in the Montreal Olympics that year. Commanding Officer Major John Bunyard was a member of the squad and when he saw Don outrun one of his Olympic team members, Danny Nightingale, it was no time at all before our Don could say goodbye to spud peeling and guard duty as he took up training with the pentathlon group - a good move. In 1978 Don won the REME Corp South East and Southern Zone steeplechase championships in 9:48 and turned in a sub-2 minute 800 metres in the same meeting. He was only the second junior rank in his corps to receive colours in athletics - the previous "squaddie" to receive such an accolade being Olympic modern pentathlete and gold medallist Jim Fox.

In 1981 it was time to put away his uniform and get back onto "civvy street". The Army had been good for Don. Ok, he had not been one for studying while at school but while serving with the REME he had gained GCE 'A' level passes in Maths and Physics and an HNC in Electronic Engineering. The electronics group Racal was now to profit from Don's talents as an engineer and later he worked for Siemens and IBM as a computer engineer.

Don had always kept in touch with Surrey AC, running for them whenever he could, and now he fell in with Pete Gilbey, Ollie Foote and Grenville Tuck. Training was a twice daily affair and they often clocked up 100 miles per week. But things were not going well for Surrey AC. They were so short of club officers that virtually every administrative task fell to Club Secretary Geoff Davis. Geoff had already approached Belgrave around 1981 to see if amalgamation could be discussed - and sure enough, in September 1982, Don and David Mote and Bob Bridges all supported Geoff and the amalgamation went ahead. The fact that the union took place just a few days ahead of Belgrave's qualifying match for the British League upset a few people (who have not forgotten it to this day!). Belgrave won that match, with Don scoring in the team, and the following year the Bels won British League Division Five. The climb to the top had begun in earnest and twenty years later, as we look back, we can see that Don played his part in all that we did - athlete, Southern League 'C' team manager, Road Running Team Manager, Road & Cross Country Team Manager, Veterans' Team Manager, minibus driver, timekeeper, field event judge and in the last few years Electric Timing Officer. He was even called upon at the Manchester Commonwealth Games to assist with the electric timing for the Triathlon.

Don met Val when she was manning a drinks station on the Belgrave '20'. Val herself supports us hugely as a field events judge and does a great deal of work for Stragglers RC - for whom Don is a second-claim member. Hercules Wimbledon AC also benefit from Don's membership as do, of course, Lauriston Runners.

Could we have a President more steeped in athletics? We don't think so! Have a great year Don - and can anyone tell us when the Club's President last ran in the National CC Champs?

items.heading: A dominating win in the semi
items.summary: Report of Belgrave's emphatic win (313 points) in the Golden Jubilee Cup semi-final at Eton on 19 July 2003, with event-by-event highlights.
items.text:
Golden Jubilee Cup

Semi Final, Eton, Eton, 19 July 2003

1 Belgrave 313; 2 Thames Valley H 207; 3 Harrow 159.5; 4 Channel Islands 146.5; 5 Crawley 140; 6 Swansea 130; 7 Havering Mayesbrook 128; 8 Woking 126.

As surprise winners of the inaugural Jubilee Cup for combined men's and women's track and field teams in 2002 we knew the opposition would be seeking to prevent a repeat Belgrave victory. However our Club had other ideas and their overwhelming superiority in the semi-final at Eton made them Cup favourites. In this match the final points total was 313 out of a possible 342. The men who have 20 events compared with the women's 18 scored 163 points out of a possible 180 (90.6%) and the women collected 150 out of a possible 162 (92.6%). However, Stuart Faben's desperately bad luck resulted in the men not turning out anyone for the javelin and instead of a certain 9 points (which would have made the men 95.6%) we scored nil. Stuart had stepped on a casually discarded bottle left lying on the track in the indoor warm-up area and sustained ligament damage. In his first track 10,000 metres Hassan Raidi gave us maximum points, and over at the long jump, Darragh O'Farrell performed right up to form to win with 7.26m.

A highly motivated (when is she anything but?) Amala Onuora prepared for her trip to Paris for the 'Youth Olympics' the following weekend by clocking 12.0 seconds in the 100m and she later anchored the winning 4 x 100m relay team. Just as Amala dominated the women's sprint, so too did Graham Beasley for the men. Julie Hollman was not best pleased with her long jump but delighted with her 1.81m high jump - a season's best. Our triple jumpers excelled with a longest ever leap from David Wellstead and a best since '96 from Caroline Stead - both aided by the stiff breeze. Double wins also came from vaulters Paul Williams and Lucy Webber - although Lucy had to share first place with a rival.

The irrepressible Maria Sharp was the unlucky person to find herself "only" in third when she tackled the 800m. Canny Kevin Nash ignored the pace of an early leader in the steeplechase and gradually overhauled him to post yet another win. Diana Holden, without a solid winter's training behind her, was not yet breaching the 50 metres barrier but it was sufficient to win. Shelley Newman in the outside throwing area did not seem to be distracted by the regular passage of cars behind the cage on the way to the overflow car park and managed 55.42 metres. In the men's throws Mick Jones and Greg Beard performed superbly with Greg's 16.17m in the shot heralding a return to form in a big way. Shot putter Eva Massey's 15.71m was not far short of her season's best. Maureen Knight placed second in the javelin where she deputised for Goldie Sayers, on Under-23 international duty in Poland

Chris Moss back on the track after his knee injury was always in control of the 800 metres. In the 200m the powerful Laurence Oboh defied anyone to pass him in a tight race and Jennifer Culley also found some tough competition in the women's event where she placed third. Jennifer later ran an unpressed anchor leg split of 56.7 seconds which helped the team to their best time of the season (3:51.2) and had earlier taken the 400 hurdles in 63.3. Rachel King, who has been running brilliantly indoors and out this year, was a class apart in the sprint hurdles where she won with 13.4 seconds as the second placed runner was still attacking the final flight of barriers. Hannah Stares took a break from the hurdles, switching to the flat 400m where she won in 55.9 - and then did it all again in the relay. Sean Baldock was able to run a couple of seconds below par to sew up the men's race.

In the longer distances the hot and breezy conditions made pace judgment difficult but Rosalie Powell coped well in the 3000m to remove nearly a quarter of a minute from her previous best. Julie Mitchell showed her usual front running approach in the combined Match 1 and 2 1500m; although outpaced in the last lap to cross the line in third, Julie was a clear Match 1 winner. Steve Sharp was masterful in the men's 1500m while Allen Graffin threw in a 64 second lap towards the end of the 5000 to ensure that he was alone for the final circuit.

items.heading: Close ! But Belgrave are Cup Winners again
items.summary: Bill Laws reports Belgrave's narrow victory over Sale Harriers Manchester in the BAL Golden Jubilee Cup Final at Bedford on 16 August 2003, with a scanned box of semi-final and final results, a team photo on page 8 and a 1500m photo (page 9's footer misprints the issue as June 2003).
items.text:
Final, Bedford, 16 August 2003

1 Belgrave 218; 2 Sale H Manchester 204; 3 Woodford Green with Essex Ladies 193; 4 Birchfield H 191; 5 Shaftesbury B 174; 6 Trafford AC 152; 7 Windsor SE&H 149; 8 Team Solent 104.

In the BAL Golden Jubilee Cup Final Birchfield fielded a strong men's team and Sale's women looking particularly threatening. With many of our stars unable to attend it would be down to everyone to put in top performances. And so it turned out as a relatively weak start left us trailing the likes of Birchfield, Sale and Woodford Green.

Mick Jones, only just back from adventures in Canada, was in the land of nod when he should have been reporting for the hammer. Fortunately Kevin Brown stepped in but his single point was lost in the discus where injury relegated him to fourth spot. At the same time junior Roy Collier was trying to tame a huge stadium pole as he equalled his pb in the pole vault; with both our main jumpers injured Roy answered a late call up.

Another late call up was Kassa Tadesse who despite lack of fitness finished an excellent second in the 10000m to signal the start of a team comeback which eventually would see us again victorious.

For the women Diana Holden threw a season's best to finish fourth in the hammer (one better than last year) and then managed a sixth place in the discus. Michelle Nestor squeezed a fifth spot in a closely contested long jump while Maureen Knight occupied the same spot in the high jump as she embarked on a busy afternoon schedule. The gradual claw back into contention was started by ever reliable Matt Douglas who stormed to our first win in the 400 hurdles. Then second for Chris Moss in an 800 which he seemed to have won but somehow his nemesis Matt Shone dipped him on the line. Graham Beasley then got another silver in the 100m to be followed by a win from Sean Baldock who dipped under 46secs for the second time this season and defeated a lacklustre Du'aine Ladejo. At about this time Ben Challenger was unlucky not to clear 2.25 in the high jump and had to settle for a first place tie with the evergreen Dalton Grant. Lucy Webber, recovering from a broken finger, battled for a valuable silver in the pole vault. In the triple jump Caroline Stead gained bronze for more valuable points.

Kevin Nash following his big breakthrough and pb at the AAA's champs, didn't disappoint. Neither too did Graham Beasley who ran a 200m pb into a headwind to soundly beat Birchfield's 400m star Daniel Caines. Not to be outdone Amy Spencer won the women's 200m and to prove she is over her injury problems ran close to a season's best. And then Stephen Sharp beat the talented Woodford junior Chris Reynolds in a sprint for the line to make the 1500m another exciting and closely contested race. In the javelin Stuart Faben struggled following his ankle injury at Eton but in the shot Greg Beard once again improved his pb to gain silver and more points. Silver too for Will Cockerell in the 5000, who has improved one place in each of the last three years in this event. With the relays to go Belgrave had moved into a small lead over Sale and Birchfield. The women's sprint relay was won by Sale but they were closely followed by the Belgrave squad. Then drama in the men's sprint relay - the baton was dropped at the first changeover but fortunately Sale were also disqualified. In the women's long relay the Belgrave squad pipped Sale thanks to a resounding second leg by Michelle Carey timed in the low 53's. And so to the last event the men's long relay with the trophy ours. Birchfield were out to salvage some pride and with Daniel Caines, Du'aine Ladejo and Bradley Yiend got within 0.05 of the Cup record. But Matt Douglas, Dan Donovan, Chris Moss and Sean Baldock got the silver and we were home and dry.

John Jeffery says he only smiles at the big matches when we are certain to lose. There were one or two grimaces early on but nothing to worry about. Great match!!!

items.heading: Another great BAL success
items.summary: Bill Laws's reports on Belgrave's 2003 Men's British Athletics League Division One title, the seventh in a row: the Division One table and accounts of all four matches (Eton 14 June, Birmingham 5 July, Eton 3 August, Wigan 30 August) with event-by-event Belgrave results and photos of Martin Dent, Stuart Faben and Tim Abeyie; on page 12 one line about the long relay is printed struck through.
items.text:
Men's British Athletics League Division One

Another great BAL success

The club registered four wins athough apart from Match 1 there were some nerve racking moments. The end result however was clear cut with another great BAL success.

Match 1 Eton 14 June 2003

Fixtures chaos hits opening match

1 Belgrave 371; 2 Newham & Essex Beagles343; 3 Birchfield 291; 4 Sale H Manchester 269; 5 Woodford Green WEL 267; 6 Windsor SE&H 236; 7 Trafford 203; 8 Shaftesbury Barnet 200

The journey to the title started very late in the season, one week before midsummer's day in fact, and fixture chaos was the talking point. Has the fixtures supremo gone mad? Well yes. Because on the same day the BMC organised a series of paced middle distance races, The AAA's ran its middle distance U20 and U23 Championships, UK Athletics held a National sprint relay squad training camp and AAA's of England had taken a team to Latvia. The atmosphere among the team managers trying to get the League off to a decent start was one of increasing frustration and suppressed anger as this joint fixture with the women's league got under way.

Kevin Brown, just back competing after injury, and 21 year old Scot Thompson, gained two seconds to start the team off to a better than expected start. Then Matt Douglas ran to a storming win in the A 400H, setting the third fastest time by a GB athlete this year in the mid 49.8's. Paul Beaumont replacing Noel Levy broke the club vets record in finishing fifth in the B event, and later substituted for Michael Parper in the B 400. The 800 saw a welcome return to these shores by Alasdair McLean Foreman, who although still jetlagged ran a very respectable 1.51.33 to gain fourth in the A race. Inter-Counties Champion Tim Bayley had equally tough competition in the B race giving too much space to Matt Shone who is also a fast finisher. In the 100 A event Lawrence Oboh's blocks slipped but Dan Donovan made amends by winning the B in his first race for the club on home shores.

The hammer, later in the programme than usual, saw John Osazuwa make a welcome return ensuring he and Mick Jones walked off with near maximum points, while on the track we gained our only maximum points (and in the steeplechase too) with Martin Dent breaking the stadium record and Kevin Nash recording his third sub 9 minute clocking of the year. Kevin also filled the B 1500 slot to back up Spencer Barden who was also out kicked by Matt Shone to finish third in the A 1500.

The Belgrave supporters led by Sir Eddie were beginning to relax as the lead stretched to 20 points. Next up was one of the closest races of the afternoon, the 110H, which the strong headwind failed to upset. Dominic Girdler finished a brilliant second to Damien Grieves but had the satisfaction of gaining Chris Baillie's scalp by the narrowest of margins. Dominic later achieved star status by running the last leg of the long relay in an official split time of 47.4 as he chased Iwan Thomas (Newham) and Chris Rawlinson (Trafford). Noteworthy too was the 47.6 split of Tim Bayley running his first one lapper since moving up to the 800.

With wins for Tim Abeyie in the A 200 and Stuart Faben in the A javelin, plus a 55m pb in the B event for Scot Thompson and a terrific 2.10 high jump from Samson Oni we moved to an invincible lead sustained by good points in the shot and triple jump.

Match 2, Birmingham, 5 July 2003

Bels and Beagles break away

1 Belgrave H 342; 2 Newham & Essex Beagles 304; 3 Woodford Green WEL 300; 4 Birchfield H 293; 5 Shaftesbury Barnet H 242; 6 Sale H Manchester 242; 7 Windsor SE&H 227; 8 Trafford AC 223.

At the end of this match it was looking like a two horse race with the Bels and Beagles breaking away from the rest of the pack. Being a team manager should come with a health warning! Once again the League clashed with a number of other high power meetings including BMC speed trials at Watford and three AAE fixtures which had been inserted into the fixtures calendar at a late date after all was thought to be done and dusted.

This time Belgrave lost seventeen of it's A team men to clashing fixtures and in some events such as the javelin and hammer where we have little depth we saw a large drop in points. But the positive side was that many of our juniors and recent juniors seized the opportunity to make their mark at the top level with Scot Thompson competing in all four throws as he concentrated on dispatching the discus sufficiently far to ensure selection for the European Under 23 Championships. Graeme Oudney and Derek Watson completed our young Scottish contingent.

Massive jams on the M6 prevented many officials reaching the venue including Simon Fennel, the match scorer with his laptop and software. Fortunately all our early competitors had stayed overnight at the local Holiday Inn where it became clear that Newham and Essex Beagles, who had reserved the same hotel, had assembled a team which could well reverse the Match 1 result.

After seven events our worst fears were confirmed - we were trailing Newham by a big margin, in spite of scoring well with a sensational double win in the long jump. Club stalwart Julian Flynn won the B event with a season's best but the star performance belonged to 18 year Onen Eyong whose spring off the board caused a lot of positive comments from fellow competitors.

It was not until mid afternoon that events turned our way signalled by Sean Baldock's victory over Du'aine Ladejo in the 400 in his season's best time. Clocking a personal best time, Dave Anderson won a truly exciting 5000 by the thickness of a vest followed by a double in the high hurdles with Dominic Girdler (also a pb) and Noel Levy who surged through to take the B race on the dip. Later Graham Beasley powered into a bend headwind to clock his season's best in the200 to be followed by Tim Benjamin emulating the win and gaining his season's best as he cruised to a fine B string victory in his first outing in Belgrave colours. However Newham were breathing down our necks with silver and bronze performances, and also did so in the sprint relay in which we recorded the fastest time since the 2001 European Clubs Cup. Then in the steeplechase, Martin Dent repeated his Match 1 victory and Simon Marwood on his debut also won, lowering his pb by six seconds. Kevin Nash with a winter's hard training behind him also clocked a pb in the 1500.

We lined up for the long relay knowing that Newham needed to win and we would have to be disqualified for Match victory to be denied. We were not let down as Michael Parper handed to Geoff Dearman (making a welcome season debut after injury) in third place - a position not relinquished on the last leg by Dan Donovan who once again doubled both relays in addition to his 100 outing.

At the end of a nail biting afternoon the general consensus was that Match 3 was going to be something special.

Match 3, Eton, 3 August 2003

Oooh! That was close

1 Belgrave H 333; 2 Newham & Essex Beagles 318; 3 Woodford Green wEL 302; 4 Birchfield H 297; 5 Sale H Manchester 266; 6 Windsor SE&H 243; 7 Shaftesbury Barnet H 228; 8 Trafford AC 180.

If we thought the last match was close then what about this one! A strong team seven days before the event deteriorated as match day approached and with athletes chasing fast times overseas, others injured, some on holiday and some simply not turning up on the day, we found ourselves under extreme pressure.

The track races started with veteran Paul Beaumont being elevated to the A 400 hurdles, and hammer thrower John Osazuwa was another to move up to an A slot with discus specialist Scot Thompson forsaking quality for quantity as he took part in all four throws in a huge effort keep us competitive.

A strong Woodford Green outfit was going great guns with Newham & Essex Beagles slowly easing up to them and an early points score had the Bels as low as sixth. It took an hour of hard grafting before we were able to move into fifth thanks to some solid running from the 400m boys with Geoff Dearman delighted to dip under 48 again and Chris Moss working his way back to the big time with his second 1:48 800 clocking of the weekend.

Seni Majekodunmi has become a triple jump first team regular in 2003 and he branched out to fill another gap - this time the high jump - where he backed up Richard Aspden and they both claimed third places. A season's best came from discus man Kevin Brown, thus ensuring that Scot Thompson scored heavily in the B. The 100 metres brought us two more third places and Darragh O'Farrell made his league debut to place fourth in the long jump with Julian Flynn heading the B competition. Another debutant, Matt Wedge, got up to 2nd in the B sprint hurdles. Greg Beard launched the shot to 17.05 metres for yet another third place having set a pb of 17.07m at Ashford the previous day.

The Bels had now moved into fourth but with the end of the match in sight, normally cheerful team managers were shaking their heads in despair. Knowing that it would be difficult to get a strong team out for the last match there were mutterings of "all over for 2003" and "goodbye to Europe for 2004". But a recovery emerged with some sparkling front running from Spencer Barden in the 1500m. A sub-59 first lap by Birchfield's Murdoch was followed by Spen pushing the pace along to 1:59 at 800m and 3:00 at 1200. Spen was still ahead with a mere 30 metres left and with Steve Sharp in close attendance, but the Sale man lunged at the line and got the verdict. We are used to seeing Graham Beasley excel in league 200s but were delighted to see 17 year-old James Ellington hold his form in the face of pressure from past European Champion Dougie Walker to clinch a super double win. Hassan Raidi attempted to go with the leaders in the 5k but faded badly over the last few laps while the more conservative Will Cockerell, bearing in mind the thirty degrees temperature, wound it up as the race progressed.

Newham were now leading the match from Woodford with Belgrave third, but it was close - and closer still after the drama of the sprint relay. The Bels were away but the Beagles dropped the baton at the second takeover. Although they recovered the stick and finished the race in last place, the last man threw down the baton in disgust and uttered an expletive in his frustration. He was disqualified for his actions - a penalty made even harsher when it was realised that both Shaftesbury and Woodford had already been DQ'd for zone infringement, meaning that the Beagles had thrown away six points.

The net result was that with two events to go Newham & Essex Beagles now led the Bels by one point!

It was Beaglers Mitchinson & Robinson versus Belgravians Nash & Marwood in the steeplechase. Kevin edged closer to Robinson who had set the pace and, still 30 metres down at the bell, closed rapidly round the turn, got to within 10 metres in the back straight, and then flew the final turn with water jump barrier untouched as he hurdled it at full speed to storm away to a seven second win. With Simon just behind Mitchison we'd come out even on points!

The management were confident of pulling off the long relay with Tim Benjamin anchoring a team of Dearman, Bayley and Osho that would surely already be leading when he took the baton - and so it proved. But now the Essex men faced another disqualification when a man clearly took the baton before the start of the takeover zone. We won in the end by 15 points having gone into the lead on the very last event - but for the DQs we'd have lost by a single point.

Match 4, Wigan 30 August 2003

Youngest ever Belgrave team clinches the title for 7th time

1 Belgrave 337; 2 Shaftesbury B 324; 3 Woodford GwEL 302; 4 Sale HM 267.5; 5 Birchfield 259; 6 Windsor SE&H 234; 7 Newham &EB 231.5; 8 Trafford 216

Confidence but not complacency was the key to the final match. With the World Championships in Paris and the World Student Games in Daegu, Korea involving several of our top athletes this last match proved once again a difficult proposition for the team management. Last year several teams could muster fewer than twenty athletes. This year we, and many of the other teams, made a determined effort to support this fixture with greater numbers. We turned to our younger members - two under-17's, four under-20's and five under-23's - to make this the youngest ever team to compete for the Club at this level. A small but elite squad of experienced seniors backed them up.

We still had gaps though, notably with nobody in the pole vault, no recognized javelin exponents, and ever game Kevin Brown serving as Mick Jones number two in the hammer. But things soon picked up with precious points in the long jump before near-maximum points in the discus followed by a high jump win from Ben Challenger who put aside his disappointment at missing out on Paris to support the team. A debut appearance in the 400m hurdles by junior Ryan Dinham followed, resulting in an excellent A string third place - a position emulated by under-23 Richard Ward in the A 800m. Adam Zawadski, back after missing the season through injury, gained maximum B string points in the 800m. Then last year's top points scorer Graham Beasley ran one of his fastest 100 metres of the season followed by an equally impressive B string win in the 200m. Sixteen year old Wade Bennett-Jackson won his debut B 100m while under-23 Tim Abeyie won the A 200m in a time only 1/100th slower than Graham's. With no specialist 400m runner present Chris Moss and Richard Ward stepped in for a handful of valuable points.

Contributing to an ultimately respectable points total were maximum points in the shot from under 23's Greg Beard and Scot Thompson. Then Spencer Barden ran away from a first class 5000m field only to repeat the feat 40 minutes later as he challenged a strong A and B combined 1500m field. Third in the A backed by Chris Moss' win in the B gained more near maximum points. Junior Jonathan Blackledge made a fine debut at BAL level getting bronze in the B 5000m. Martin Dent fresh from more European travels still had enough fitness to finish second to Stuart Stokes in the 3000 steeplechase.

And the final icing on the cake was an attack on the GB Club junior 4 x 100m relay record (41.32) by a Belgrave squad comprising of Wade Bennett-Jackson, Laurence Oboh, James Ellington and Set Osho. They finished second to a strong Shaftesbury team and only just missed the record. And so another league win - the seventh consecutive one to add to our earlier Jubilee Cup victory.

items.text:
BAL Points scorers 2003

With so many conflicting meetings throughout the season (all of which attracted the support of many of our A team men) it took 55 athletes to ensure Belgrave's 7th consecutive British League victory. And the most surprising and rewarding feature was that it was several of our younger members, fresh from the junior ranks, who made major contributions to a win which will ensure that once again we represent the best of British Clubs in the European Champion Clubs' Championships in 2004.

The top ten in our rankings showed a big change from previous years with only Spencer Barden, Graham Beasley, Kevin Brown and Julian Flynn of our big guns producing the goods. New member Dan Donovan made an impressive start while under 23 year olds Scot Thompson, Greg Beard, Seni Majekodunmi, and Dominic Girdler made significant contributions.

But it was Scot Thompson, taking advantage of vacancies to throw hammer, shot, javelin and discus to accumulate a points score, which not only eliminated the record set by Jon Ridgeon of 113 points in 1992, but also raised it to a level unlikely to be surpassed for many a year.

At the other end of the youth spectrum veteran Paul Beaumont returned after an absence from the top ranks to add significantly to his all-time points total. All this has meant a big change to the all-time Rankings List which will be updated and published in the near future

items.summary: Rex Bale reports the Belgrave women's win in the UK Women's League qualifying match at Abingdon on 13 September 2003, with run-on Belgrave results and a photo of shot putter Eva Massey; the first line of the photo caption is printed struck through.
items.text:
Southern Women's League Division One

UKWL Qualifying Match, Abingdon, 13 September 2003

Belles win the qualifer

1 Belgrave 234; 2 Cardiff 175; 3 Pitreavie 168; 4 Blackheath & Bromley 160; 5 Blackpool 149; 6 Cannock & Stafford 122; 7 Deeside 111; 8 Basingstoke &MH 9.

Although finishing in the basement of the Womens Southern League the senior women were successful in gaining a place in the qualifying match for the UK Women's League. And so after a long hard season the team had to lift themselves once more to try to join the top tier. Many of the elite athletes did not appear and so the majority of the team was composed of the 'regulars'. It was typical of their dedication that they worked so hard for what in the end turned out to be a comfortable win.

The match was well organised with a good commentator and an efficient result service to the extent that the top performaces were given UKA grades. Hence we learnt that Diana Holden's 52.88 in the hammer, Lucy Webber's 3.40 in the pole vault, and Eva Massey's 14.98 in the shot were all Grade 1 performances. Eva also managed a Grade 2 in the discus, surprising us all with a 40 metres plus throw to win the A competition.

Maureen Knight, 'fresh' from gaining a silver medal in the British Isles Combined Events Cup, won the high jump A, the javelin B and was only a fraction below her season's best of 11.47 in a high calibre triple jump competition where the first four achieved grade 2 jumps.

Jennifer Culley and Amala Onoura teamed up for the flat sprints and gained double seconds in the 100m. Jennifer won the 200 B and was second in the 400 hurdles but was spared doing a leg of the 4 x 400m relay since the team took a well earned rest realising that they had done the business in style. Michelle Carey, who has been in top form recently, was a clear winner in the 400 A race and helped the 4 x 100m relay to second place. In this race Andrea Abrams, now 32, answering a late call-up to help the team out, showed no signs of rustiness and also took second place in the B jump with over 5 metres. Ann Hollman was B winner in both shot put and high jump and gained third place in the javelin A. Michelle Nestor won the B triple jump and was third in the A long jump.

The trio of middle distance races was the weakest area but nevertheless there were valuable points to be gained here particularly as some of the teams did not field runners. It was fitting that an unwell Jacqui Smiter with over 100 Southern League team appearances to her credit turned out in the 800m to help the team, as did Jo Patterson and Mathilde Heaton.

Then there was ever-reliable Hannah Stares who has been in super hurdling form and won both the 400mH B and 100mH A races, and for good measure the flat 400m B as well; her lap hurdle time of 61.3 seconds was almost identical to Jennifer's, both grade 2 performances.

Team manager Cynthia James led by example in the first event and although her body protested at swinging the 4 kilogram weight her competitive spirit got the better of her and rather than just lob it just outside the cage she managed 15 metres to beat two rivals for third place.

Got your number (118 118)

Rex Bale was set up by top W50 runner Ros Tabor, entries secretary for the Dulwich 10k (12 October), who gave him the number 118 along with a promotional postcard for this part of the new 'Directory Enquiries' system. At the race start, just when he was thinking he should have hired a wig and bought a pair of red socks to wear, along came long standing Belgravian, postman Peter Cross. He was the one who should have been given this number, since with his 60's style haircut and drooping moustache he is the young David Bedford lookalike. He has become known simply as 118 at work, and poor Peter has to put up with 'Hello 118' and 'Got your number !' from lorry drivers, even when he is not in his running gear ! After the race they exchanged numbers so that Peter, who has run over 90 half marathons and runs some of his races with his daughter for company, can really look the part.
